questions.question: What are the layers of Clean Architecture and what is the Dependency Rule?
questions.title: Clean Architecture Layers and the Dependency Rule
questions.direct_answer: Clean Architecture (Robert C. Martin, 2012) organizes code as **four concentric circles** — from the inside out: **Entities** (enterprise business rules), **Use Cases** (application business rules), **Interface Adapters** (controllers, presenters, gateways), and **Frameworks & Drivers** (Spring, JPA, web, DB). The **Dependency Rule** states: **source code dependencies must point only inward**. Inner circles know nothing about outer circles. Cross the boundary inward via interfaces; cross outward via dependency inversion. Result: domain logic is testable, framework-free, and survives infrastructure changes.

interviewer_intent.testing: The four layers and what belongs in each, the strict inward-only dependency rule, and the dependency-inversion mechanic that lets inner circles trigger outer ones without depending on them.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Putting framework annotations in entities or use cases, or letting use cases import from interface adapters.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Discuss when the four-circle model is overkill (small CRUD), pragmatic packaging (3 packages instead of 4 layers), and how it relates to Hexagonal/Onion.

sections.title: The Four Circles
sections.content:
From innermost to outermost:

**1. Entities (innermost):**
- Enterprise-wide business rules and invariants.
- Plain objects, no framework, no annotations.
- Survive any application: a `Money` value object or `BankAccount` aggregate would be the same in any of the company's apps.
- Example: `Account.withdraw(amount)` enforcing 'cannot overdraft.'

**2. Use Cases:**
- Application-specific business rules — the orchestration of entities for *this* application's user goals.
- One class per user goal: `PlaceOrder`, `RefundOrder`, `CancelSubscription`.
- Calls entities; depends on abstract interfaces (`OrderRepository`, `PaymentGateway`) defined here, implemented outside.

**3. Interface Adapters:**
- Controllers (translate HTTP → use case input).
- Presenters (translate use case output → HTTP response).
- Gateways (implement repository / external API interfaces from the use-case layer).
- This is where DTOs and JPA entities live.

**4. Frameworks & Drivers (outermost):**
- Spring, JPA, the web framework, the DB driver, message brokers, file system.
- 'Glue' code; configuration; infrastructure details.
- Should be the most volatile and easiest to swap.

sections.title: The Dependency Rule
sections.content:
**Source code dependencies must point only inward.**

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    F[Frameworks & Drivers]
    IA[Interface Adapters]
    UC[Use Cases]
    E[Entities]
    F --> IA --> UC --> E
```

- Use Cases can import Entities. ✅
- Entities cannot import Use Cases. ❌
- Interface Adapters can import Use Cases and Entities. ✅
- Use Cases cannot import Interface Adapters. ❌
- Frameworks know about everything inward; nothing inward knows about Frameworks.

**No Spring annotations on Entities or Use Cases.** No JPA `@Entity` on domain objects. No `@RestController` reach-through into use-case logic.

**Why:** the inner circles are stable; they shouldn't change because some outer detail (Postgres → MongoDB) changed. Inner-to-outer would create coupling that breaks this stability.

sections.title: Crossing Boundaries Outward — Dependency Inversion
Crossing Boundaries Inward
Pragmatic Packaging
sections.content:
Four formal layers can over-engineer small projects. Common pragmatic structure for a Spring Boot service:

```
com.example.orders/
  domain/                          -- entities + value objects (innermost)
    Order.java
    OrderItem.java
  application/                     -- use cases + ports
    PlaceOrderUseCase.java
    OrderRepository.java
    PaymentGateway.java
  adapter/
    in/web/                        -- controllers, DTOs
      OrderController.java
    out/persistence/               -- JPA gateway, mappers
      JpaOrderRepository.java
      OrderJpaEntity.java
    out/payment/
      StripePaymentGateway.java
  config/                          -- Spring @Configuration (outermost)
    BeansConfig.java
```

Three practical layers map cleanly to four formal ones; the dependency rule is enforced by package dependencies (ArchUnit can verify in CI).

sections.title: Clean vs Hexagonal vs Onion
sections.content:
All three are the same family with slight differences:

| Pattern | Author | Distinctive trait |
|---|---|---|
| Hexagonal | Cockburn (2005) | Ports & adapters terminology |
| Onion | Palermo (2008) | Layers as concentric circles |
| Clean | Martin (2012) | Four named circles + explicit Use Case layer |

In practice: same dependency rule (inward-only), same use of interfaces for inversion, same domain-at-center mindset. Pick whichever vocabulary your team prefers; what matters is consistency.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Spring annotations in domain/use case.** `@Service`, `@Component`, `@Transactional` belong outside the inner circles. Use plain constructor injection wired by `@Configuration`.
- **JPA `@Entity` on domain objects.** Domain entities are pure; map to JPA entities in the persistence adapter.
- **Use cases imported by entities.** Backwards. Entities are pure data + invariants.
- **One use case = one HTTP endpoint dogma.** Use cases model user goals; one goal can have multiple endpoints (REST + admin + CLI).
- **Forgetting presenters.** Returning domain objects from controllers leaks the domain to clients. Convert via DTO/presenter at the boundary.
- **Treating Clean as gospel for tiny services.** A 4-endpoint CRUD doesn't need 12 use case classes. Layered is fine for those.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Four circles:** Entities, Use Cases, Interface Adapters, Frameworks & Drivers.
- **Dependency Rule:** source dependencies point only inward.
- **Inversion:** inner layers define interfaces; outer layers implement.
- **No framework annotations** on entities or use cases.
- **Controllers + presenters + gateways** live in interface adapters.
- **Three-package pragmatic structure** (domain, application, adapter) is fine for most projects.
- **Clean ≈ Hexagonal ≈ Onion** — same family, different vocabulary.
- **ArchUnit** to enforce dependency rule in CI.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
**The four circles**

Innermost to outermost: Entities, Use Cases, Interface Adapters, Frameworks & Drivers.

Entities: enterprise-wide business rules and invariants. Plain objects, no framework. Survive any app — a Money value object or BankAccount aggregate same in any of the company's apps.

Use Cases: application-specific business rules. Orchestration of entities for this app's user goals. One class per user goal: PlaceOrder, RefundOrder. Depends on abstract interfaces (OrderRepository) defined here, implemented outside.

Interface Adapters: controllers (translate HTTP → use case input), presenters (use case output → HTTP response), gateways (implement repository/external API interfaces). DTOs and JPA entities live here.

Frameworks & Drivers: Spring, JPA, web framework, DB driver. Glue and configuration. Most volatile, easiest to swap.

**The Dependency Rule**

Source code dependencies must point only inward.

- Use Cases can import Entities. Entities cannot import Use Cases.
- Interface Adapters can import Use Cases. Use Cases cannot import Interface Adapters.
- Frameworks know about everything inward; nothing inward knows about frameworks.

No Spring annotations on Entities or Use Cases. No JPA @Entity on domain objects.

Why: inner circles are stable; shouldn't change because Postgres → Mongo. Inner-to-outer dependency would break this stability.

**Crossing boundaries outward — dependency inversion**

Use cases must call DB but can't import it. Solved by inversion: define interface in the inner layer, implement in the outer layer.

OrderRepository owned by use cases. PlaceOrderUseCase depends on it. JpaOrderGateway in adapter layer implements it.

Dependency arrow: adapter → use case (inward). Runtime data flow: use case → adapter via interface. Spring @Configuration wires the implementation at startup.

**Crossing inward**

OrderController in interface adapters: knows Spring + use cases. Calls placeOrder.place() with plain Java args (no HttpServletRequest). Use case returns domain object; presenter (OrderResponse.from) converts to HTTP shape. Use case has no idea HTTP exists.

**Pragmatic packaging**

Three practical packages: domain (entities + value objects), application (use cases + ports), adapter (in/web for controllers, out/persistence for JPA, out/payment for Stripe). Plus config for Spring @Configuration.

Maps cleanly to the four formal layers. ArchUnit enforces dependency rule in CI.

**Clean vs Hexagonal vs Onion**

Same family. Hexagonal (Cockburn 2005) ports & adapters terminology. Onion (Palermo 2008) concentric circles. Clean (Martin 2012) four named circles, explicit Use Case layer.

Same dependency rule, same interface inversion, same domain-at-center. Pick vocabulary your team prefers; consistency matters more than label.

**Common mistakes**

- @Service, @Transactional in inner circles — belongs outside
- JPA @Entity on domain objects — map in persistence adapter
- Use cases imported by entities — backwards
- One use case = one endpoint dogma — user goals can have multiple endpoints (REST + admin + CLI)
- Returning domain objects from controllers — use presenters/DTOs
- Clean as gospel for tiny services — 4-endpoint CRUD is fine layered

**Recommendation**

**Apply Clean Architecture for non-trivial Spring Boot services with rich domain logic, multiple input adapters (HTTP + Kafka + scheduled), or strict testability needs. Use the pragmatic three-package structure (domain / application / adapter); don't over-engineer with four formal layers in small services. Keep entities and use cases free of Spring/JPA annotations — wire dependencies in @Configuration. Enforce the dependency rule with ArchUnit in CI. For simple CRUD, stick with classic layered — Clean's complexity isn't free.**

questions.question: How do you implement the Use Case / Interactor pattern in Java?
questions.title: Use Case / Interactor Pattern in Java
questions.direct_answer: A **Use Case (also called an Interactor)** is a class that **encapsulates one application-specific user goal** — e.g., `PlaceOrderUseCase`, `RefundOrderUseCase`. It receives a request DTO (or arguments), orchestrates entities and gateways, and returns a response DTO. Each use case has **one public method** (`execute`/`handle`/`place`), depends on **interfaces (ports) it owns**, and contains **no framework code**. This makes use cases unit-testable in isolation, callable from any input adapter (HTTP, Kafka, CLI), and the natural unit of granularity for an application.

interviewer_intent.testing: Use case as one-class-one-goal, the input/output DTO model, dependency injection via constructor, and how use cases differ from a traditional Spring @Service.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Use cases that handle HTTP concerns directly, or 'fat' use cases that do five unrelated things, or shoving all CRUD into one 'OrderService' use case.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Discuss input/output ports (Cockburn's terminology), command vs query use cases, transaction boundaries on use cases, and the trade-off vs traditional service classes.

sections.title: What a Use Case Is
sections.content:
A use case represents **one user goal**: 'Place an order', 'Refund an order', 'Send a password reset email'. It is the unit of application behavior that the business cares about.

In code:
- One class per use case.
- One public method (`execute`, `handle`, or a verb that names the goal: `place(...)`, `refund(...)`).
- Dependencies (repositories, gateways, other use cases) injected via the constructor.
- Pure Java; no Spring annotations on the class itself (Spring wires it via `@Configuration`).

**Compared to a traditional Spring `@Service`:**
- A `OrderService` typically has 10 methods (`place`, `cancel`, `refund`, `findById`, `markShipped`, ...).
- A use case set has 10 classes: `PlaceOrderUseCase`, `CancelOrderUseCase`, etc.
- More files, but each file does exactly one thing, has explicit dependencies for that one thing, and tests in isolation.

sections.title: Skeleton Implementation
Adapters Around the Use Case
Command vs Query Use Cases
sections.content:
Following CQRS-style separation:

**Command use cases** (mutate state):
- `PlaceOrderUseCase`, `RefundOrderUseCase`, `CancelOrderUseCase`.
- Often transactional.
- Return minimal output (id, status).

**Query use cases** (read-only):
- `GetOrderHistoryUseCase`, `SearchOrdersUseCase`.
- Often `@Transactional(readOnly = true)`.
- Return rich DTOs tailored to the query (presenter shape).
- Can bypass the domain model for performance — query directly against read models / SQL projections.

Keeping them separate prevents 'OrderService' from becoming a 50-method beast and makes clear which operations have side effects.

sections.title: Transactions on Use Cases
Testing Use Cases in Isolation
Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Use case method takes `HttpServletRequest`.** Couples to HTTP; use a plain command DTO.
- **Multiple methods per use case.** `OrderUseCase.place(...)` and `.cancel(...)` and `.refund(...)` is just an `OrderService` in disguise. Split.
- **Use case calls another use case directly.** Acceptable sometimes, but often a sign you're missing a domain service or that the second use case should be a private helper.
- **No DTO at the boundary.** Returning a JPA entity or a domain entity bypasses the adapter layer's responsibility.
- **Spring annotations on the use case class.** `@Service`, `@Autowired field injection` — makes the use case framework-coupled.
- **Use cases for trivial CRUD.** A pure `GetUserById` is just a `userRepo.findById(id)` away — wrapping in a use case adds ceremony without value. Reserve use cases for cases with real business logic.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Use case = one class per user goal.**
- **One public method**, named after the verb of the goal.
- **Input DTO + output DTO** at the boundary.
- **Depends on interfaces (ports) it owns**; implemented in adapter layer.
- **No framework code** in the use case class; wire via `@Configuration`.
- **Same use case callable from HTTP, Kafka, CLI** — input adapter agnostic.
- **Transactions on the use case**, not controller, not repository.
- **Trivial to unit-test** with in-memory ports.
- **Reserve for cases with real business logic;** pure CRUD doesn't need a use case wrapper.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
**What a use case is**

One user goal: 'Place an order', 'Refund an order'. The unit of application behavior the business cares about.

In code: one class per use case, one public method named after the verb, dependencies (repositories, gateways) injected via constructor, pure Java without Spring annotations on the class itself.

Compared to traditional Spring @Service: an OrderService typically has 10 methods (place, cancel, refund, ...). A use case set has 10 classes. More files, but each does one thing with explicit dependencies, tests in isolation.

**Skeleton**

Input port: PlaceOrderUseCase interface with one method.
Input DTO (command): PlaceOrderCommand record with customerId, items, idempotencyKey.
Output DTO: PlaceOrderResponse with orderId, total, placedAt.
Output ports: OrderRepository, InventoryGateway interfaces owned by the use case layer.
Implementation: PlaceOrderInteractor implements PlaceOrderUseCase, depends on the ports via constructor.

Logic: idempotency check, domain logic via entities, persist. Zero Spring imports. Wired by @Configuration, called by @RestController adapter.

**Adapters around it**

Same use case can be called from REST controller (HTTP request → build command → placeOrder.place(cmd) → response) or from Kafka consumer (event → build command → placeOrder.place(cmd)). The use case doesn't care which one called it.

**Command vs query use cases**

Command use cases (mutate state): PlaceOrderUseCase, RefundOrderUseCase. Often transactional. Return minimal output.

Query use cases (read-only): GetOrderHistoryUseCase, SearchOrdersUseCase. @Transactional(readOnly=true). Return rich DTOs tailored to the query. Can bypass domain model for performance, query directly against read models.

Separation prevents 'OrderService' from becoming a 50-method beast.

**Transactions on use cases**

Use case is the natural transaction boundary: one user goal = one business transaction.

Pattern A: AOP/proxy wrap in @Configuration. Pure but heavier.
Pattern B (pragmatic): @Transactional on the implementation. Less pure but commonly accepted.
Pattern C (purist): UnitOfWork interface in inner layer; Spring-backed implementation in adapter.

Boundary is the use case, not the controller and not the repository.

**Testing**

Dependencies are interfaces, class is plain Java. Test with in-memory port implementations. No Spring context. No DB. No Testcontainers. Tests run in milliseconds.

**Common mistakes**

- Use case takes HttpServletRequest — couples to HTTP; use plain command DTO
- Multiple methods per use case — just OrderService in disguise; split
- Use case calls another use case directly — sometimes OK, often a missing domain service
- No DTO at boundary — returning JPA/domain entity bypasses adapter responsibility
- Spring annotations on use case class — framework-coupled
- Use cases for trivial CRUD — GetUserById is just userRepo.findById; wrapping is ceremony without value

**Recommendation**

**Use the Use Case pattern when business logic is non-trivial, when multiple input adapters share the same operation, or when fast pure-unit testability is critical. One class per user goal, command + response DTOs, depend on inner-owned ports, wire with @Configuration, transactions at the use case boundary. For trivial CRUD operations the wrapper is overhead — a controller calling a repository directly is fine. Reserve use cases for behavior that has real orchestration, validation, or side effects worth isolating.**

questions.question: How do you organize a Spring Boot project following Clean Architecture principles?
questions.title: Spring Boot Project Structure for Clean Architecture
questions.direct_answer: Organize a Spring Boot Clean Architecture project around **three (or four) packages by responsibility, not by technical layer:** `domain` (entities + value objects), `application` (use cases + ports), `adapter` (in/web, out/persistence, out/external). Spring Boot lives in the `adapter` packages and a `config` package; the `domain` and `application` packages have **zero Spring imports**. Wire dependencies via `@Configuration` beans. Enforce package boundaries with **ArchUnit** in CI. Optionally split into Maven/Gradle modules for compile-time enforcement.

interviewer_intent.testing: Practical packaging that enforces Clean Architecture's dependency rule, where Spring fits, and how to enforce boundaries automatically.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Spring annotations leaking into domain/application packages, or one giant `service` package with everything mixed.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Multi-module Maven setup for compile-time boundary enforcement, ArchUnit rules, and the trade-off vs single-module pragmatic structure.

sections.title: Recommended Single-Module Structure
sections.content:
```
src/main/java/com/example/orders/
  domain/                          -- Entities + Value Objects (innermost)
    Order.java
    OrderItem.java
    Money.java
  application/                     -- Use Cases + Ports
    port/in/
      PlaceOrderUseCase.java
      CancelOrderUseCase.java
      command/
        PlaceOrderCommand.java
      response/
        PlaceOrderResponse.java
    port/out/
      OrderRepository.java
      InventoryGateway.java
      PaymentGateway.java
    service/
      PlaceOrderInteractor.java
      CancelOrderInteractor.java
  adapter/
    in/web/                        -- Inbound HTTP adapter
      OrderController.java
      dto/CreateOrderRequest.java
      dto/OrderResponse.java
      ApiExceptionHandler.java
    in/messaging/                  -- Inbound Kafka adapter
      OrderCommandConsumer.java
    out/persistence/               -- Outbound DB adapter
      JpaOrderRepository.java
      OrderJpaEntity.java
      OrderMapper.java
    out/payment/                   -- Outbound payment adapter
      StripePaymentGateway.java
  config/                          -- Spring wiring (outermost)
    BeansConfig.java
    SecurityConfig.java
```

**Rules:**
- `domain` imports nothing from `application`, `adapter`, `config`.
- `application` imports only from `domain`.
- `adapter` imports from `application` (uses ports) and `domain` (uses entities).
- `config` imports from everywhere; assembles beans.

sections.title: Where Spring Lives
Persistence Adapter — JPA Without Polluting the Domain
Multi-Module Maven — Compile-Time Enforcement
sections.content:
For larger teams, split into Maven/Gradle modules so the compiler enforces boundaries:

```
order-service/
  pom.xml                          -- aggregator
  domain/
    pom.xml                        -- depends on: nothing
  application/
    pom.xml                        -- depends on: domain
  adapter-in-web/
    pom.xml                        -- depends on: application, spring-web
  adapter-in-messaging/
    pom.xml                        -- depends on: application, spring-kafka
  adapter-out-persistence/
    pom.xml                        -- depends on: application, spring-data-jpa
  adapter-out-payment/
    pom.xml                        -- depends on: application, http-client
  bootstrap/
    pom.xml                        -- depends on: all adapters + spring-boot-starter
```

- `domain` cannot import Spring — not on the classpath.
- `application` cannot import a concrete adapter — adapters depend on it, not vice versa.
- `bootstrap` is the assembled application; runs Spring's `@SpringBootApplication`.

**Cost:** more poms / build configuration. **Benefit:** boundary violations are compile errors, not runtime ones.

sections.title: Enforcing the Dependency Rule with ArchUnit
Testing Strategy by Layer
sections.content:
**Domain tests:** plain JUnit, no Spring, no DB. Test entity invariants and value-object behavior.

**Use case tests:** plain JUnit. Inject in-memory implementations of ports. Test orchestration, business rules, error paths. Run in milliseconds.

**Adapter tests:**
- Web: `@WebMvcTest` (Spring slice, no full context). Verify HTTP ↔ use-case-DTO mapping.
- Persistence: Testcontainers + real Postgres + the JPA adapter. Verify mappings + queries.
- External (payment, email): WireMock for HTTP gateways; in-memory for simpler ones.

**Integration tests (`@SpringBootTest`):** sparingly, for end-to-end smoke tests of critical flows. Most logic already covered by faster slice/unit tests.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Package by technical layer instead of by responsibility:** `controllers/`, `services/`, `repositories/` mixes domains; lose locality.
- **Spring annotations leaking inward.** `@Service` on the interactor or `@Entity` on the domain object — inner circles depend on Spring/JPA.
- **One giant `application` package** without sub-packages by feature — hard to navigate as the project grows.
- **JPA entities reused as domain entities** to avoid mappers. Saves 1 file but couples schema to domain.
- **No CI enforcement of boundaries.** Without ArchUnit / module split, the discipline drifts in PRs.
- **Putting bootstrap (`@SpringBootApplication`) in `application`.** Belongs in `bootstrap` / `config`.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Package by responsibility** (`domain`, `application`, `adapter`, `config`), not by technical layer.
- **Domain and application are framework-free.**
- **Adapter packages contain Spring annotations** (`@RestController`, `@Repository`).
- **Wire ports to implementations in `@Configuration`.**
- **JPA entities live in persistence adapter,** not in the domain.
- **Multi-module Maven** for compile-time boundary enforcement; ArchUnit for single-module.
- **Test by layer:** plain JUnit for domain + use case; slices for adapters; minimal `@SpringBootTest` for end-to-end.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
**Recommended single-module structure**

Package by responsibility, not technical layer:

- domain/ — Entities + Value Objects (innermost). Order, OrderItem, Money. No imports from anywhere else.
- application/ — Use Cases + Ports. port/in for use case interfaces + commands/responses, port/out for repository/gateway interfaces, service/ for interactors. Imports only from domain.
- adapter/ — in/web for controllers, in/messaging for Kafka consumers, out/persistence for JPA gateway, out/payment for Stripe. Imports application + domain.
- config/ — Spring wiring. @Configuration with @Bean factories. Imports from everywhere.

**Where Spring lives**

Spring annotations only in adapter and config. @RestController, @KafkaListener in adapter/in/. @Repository in adapter/out/. @Configuration, @Bean in config/.

Domain and application are pure Java. Entities are records or POJOs (no @Entity). Use cases are plain classes with constructor injection (no @Service). Ports are interfaces with no annotations.

Wiring: @Bean factory in @Configuration creates new PlaceOrderInteractor(orderRepo, inventory). Spring sees the @Bean and wires the implementation it finds for each port.

**Persistence adapter — JPA without polluting domain**

Domain Order is a record. OrderJpaEntity is a separate @Entity-annotated class with @Table, @Id, @OneToMany. OrderSpringRepo extends JpaRepository<OrderJpaEntity>. JpaOrderRepository implements OrderRepository (the port), uses OrderMapper to convert between domain Order and OrderJpaEntity.

Schema changes in JPA don't touch the domain.

**Multi-module Maven**

For larger teams: separate modules domain/, application/, adapter-in-web/, adapter-out-persistence/, adapter-out-payment/, bootstrap/. Domain depends on nothing. Application depends on domain. Adapters depend on application + their framework. Bootstrap depends on all.

Domain literally cannot import Spring — not on the classpath. Adapters cannot bypass application. Boundary violations become compile errors, not runtime ones.

Cost: more poms. Benefit: enforcement at compile time.

**Enforcing with ArchUnit (single-module)**

Tests like noClasses().that().resideInAPackage('..domain..').should().dependOnClassesThat().resideInAnyPackage('..application..', '..adapter..', 'org.springframework..').

Verify @RestController only in adapter/in/web, etc. Run in CI; broken architecture fails the build.

**Testing strategy by layer**

Domain tests: plain JUnit, no Spring, no DB. Test entity invariants.
Use case tests: plain JUnit, in-memory port implementations. Test orchestration, business rules, error paths. Milliseconds.
Web adapter: @WebMvcTest slice. Verify HTTP ↔ use-case-DTO mapping.
Persistence adapter: Testcontainers + real Postgres. Verify mappings + queries.
External: WireMock for HTTP gateways.
Integration: minimal @SpringBootTest for end-to-end smoke tests of critical flows.

**Common mistakes**

- Package by technical layer (controllers/, services/, repositories/) — mixes domains, loses locality
- Spring annotations leaking inward — @Service on interactor, @Entity on domain object
- One giant application package without feature sub-packages
- JPA entities reused as domain entities to avoid mappers — saves a file, couples schema to domain
- No CI enforcement — without ArchUnit/module split, discipline drifts in PRs
- @SpringBootApplication in application — belongs in bootstrap/config

**Recommendation**

**Default to a three-package single-module structure (domain / application / adapter / config) for most Spring Boot Clean Architecture projects. Keep domain and application framework-free; wire dependencies via @Configuration. Enforce boundaries with ArchUnit in CI. Graduate to a multi-module Maven setup once the team is large enough that compile-time enforcement saves more time than it costs in build configuration. Map JPA entities separately from domain entities — the small mapping tax buys schema independence and clean tests.**

questions.question: What is the difference between a rich domain model and an anemic domain model?
questions.title: Rich vs Anemic Domain Model
questions.direct_answer: An **anemic domain model** has data classes (just getters/setters) and **all business logic in service classes** — the objects don't enforce their own invariants, and the same logic is often duplicated or scattered. A **rich domain model** has objects that **own both data and the behavior that operates on it** — invariants enforced inside the entity, validation in the constructor, business operations as methods on the object. Rich models reduce bugs from invalid state, make the code self-documenting, and pair naturally with DDD; anemic models are the default in many Spring CRUD apps and become unmanageable as business logic grows.

interviewer_intent.testing: Why putting business logic in service methods (anemic) leads to inconsistent state and scattered rules, and how rich models prevent that by encapsulating invariants.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Defending anemic models because 'JPA needs setters' — it doesn't (use protected setters or builder); or building 'rich' models that just expose more methods on a still-anemic object.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Discuss tell-don't-ask, encapsulation invariants in constructors, value objects, and how rich models map cleanly to DDD aggregates.

sections.title: The Two Models Side by Side
Why Anemic Hurts at Scale
sections.content:
**Scattered business rules.** The 'cannot cancel shipped order' rule lives in `OrderService.cancel`. The same rule exists in `RefundService.refund` and in `AdminCancelService.adminCancel`. Three places, three risks of drift.

**Invalid state is reachable.** `order.setStatus(OrderStatus.SHIPPED)` followed by `order.setTotal(BigDecimal.ZERO)` from anywhere produces a meaningless object. No compiler or runtime check stops it.

**Tell, don't ask, lost.** Anemic forces every caller to ask the object for data, then make decisions outside it. Rich models tell the object what to do and let it decide.

**Service classes balloon.** As features grow, OrderService becomes 2,000 lines. Refactoring becomes risky.

**Hard to test in isolation.** You need the service + the entity + the repository to test 'cannot cancel shipped'. A rich model makes that one assertion on a constructed entity.

**Duplicated derived state.** `total` cached in the entity but also recalculated in services — they drift apart in production.

sections.title: What Rich Models Give You
sections.content:
**Invariants in the constructor.** An object cannot exist in an invalid state. If it's constructed, it's valid. This is the single most powerful guarantee in OOP.

**Self-documenting.** `order.cancel()` makes the intent obvious; `orderService.cancel(order)` doesn't say where the rules live.

**Centralized logic.** All cancel rules in `Order.cancel()`. Change once, applies everywhere.

**Composable.** `order.cancel(); refunds.process(order);` reads like the use case description.

**Easier testing.** Test the entity in isolation with plain JUnit; no Spring.

**Aligns with DDD aggregates.** Aggregates *must* enforce invariants; rich models are the implementation.

sections.title: JPA Doesn't Force Anemic — Common Excuse Refuted
When Anemic Is Actually Fine
sections.content:
Not every class needs to be rich:

**DTOs:** transfer data across boundaries (HTTP request, Kafka message). Pure data, no behavior. Use records.

**Read models / projections:** built from events for queries. Pure data; the query API is the behavior.

**Trivial CRUD entities** (a `Country` lookup table with `code` and `name`). No invariants beyond non-null; no behavior makes sense. Anemic is honest here.

**Configuration / metadata objects.** Static, immutable, no rules.

The smell isn't 'class without behavior' — it's 'class with behavior elsewhere that should be on it.'

sections.title: The Tell-Don't-Ask Heuristic
sections.content:
The classic test for anemic vs rich:

**Asking (anemic):**
```java
if (order.getStatus() == OrderStatus.PENDING && order.getItems().size() > 0) {
    order.setStatus(OrderStatus.SUBMITTED);
    order.setSubmittedAt(Instant.now());
}
```
Caller asks for data, decides, mutates. Rules outside the object.

**Telling (rich):**
```java
order.submit();   // validates internally; throws if invalid
```
Caller tells the object what to do. Rules live with the data.

If your services are full of `if (entity.getX() == ...) entity.setY(...)` blocks, the entity is anemic and your service is doing the entity's job.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Calling something rich because it has methods.** A class with `getStatus`, `setStatus`, and `isShipped()` is still anemic if `isShipped()` is just `return status == SHIPPED`.
- **Using setters from anywhere.** Even with public methods like `cancel()`, leaving `setStatus(OrderStatus s)` public lets callers bypass invariants.
- **Splitting one aggregate's logic across multiple objects.** Order rules in `Order` and `OrderHelper` and `OrderValidator` defeats encapsulation.
- **Putting persistence concerns in business methods.** `order.cancel()` shouldn't call `orderRepo.save(this)`; the use case orchestrates persistence.
- **Treating value objects as 'too small to bother.'** `Money(amount, currency)` enforcing that you can't add USD to EUR is the textbook value-object win.
- **Refactoring to rich models without DDD intent.** Just renaming methods doesn't fix poorly modeled aggregates.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Anemic:** data classes + service-class logic. **Rich:** data + behavior on the same object.
- **Rich models enforce invariants in constructors and operations** — invalid state unreachable.
- **Anemic scatters rules across services** and duplicates them.
- **Tell, don't ask:** rich models accept commands, not data extraction.
- **JPA doesn't force anemic;** use protected setters or separate domain entities from JPA entities.
- **DTOs, read models, and trivial lookup tables can stay anemic** — not everything needs behavior.
- **Rich models pair with DDD aggregates** — they're the implementation of the rules.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
**The two models side by side**

Anemic: Order has only getters/setters; OrderService has all the logic. orderService.cancel(o) checks status, mutates fields. Order can be put into invalid state from anywhere because setters are exposed.

Rich: Order is constructed valid (invariants in constructor), exposes public business methods (cancel(), addItem()), no setters. order.total cannot be set wrong because there's no setter — it's recomputed from items every time.

**Why anemic hurts at scale**

- Scattered business rules: 'cannot cancel shipped' lives in OrderService.cancel, RefundService.refund, AdminCancelService.adminCancel. Three places, three risks of drift
- Invalid state reachable: setStatus(SHIPPED) then setTotal(0) produces meaningless object
- Tell-don't-ask lost: every caller asks for data, decides outside
- Service classes balloon: OrderService becomes 2000 lines
- Hard to test in isolation
- Duplicated derived state: total cached in entity also recalculated in services, drifts in production

**What rich models give you**

- Invariants in constructor: object cannot exist in invalid state. If it's constructed, it's valid. Most powerful OOP guarantee
- Self-documenting: order.cancel() obvious, orderService.cancel(order) doesn't say where the rules live
- Centralized logic: change once, applies everywhere
- Composable: order.cancel(); refunds.process(order); reads like the use case
- Easier testing: plain JUnit on the entity
- Aligns with DDD aggregates

**JPA doesn't force anemic**

Myth: 'JPA needs public setters; therefore entities must be anemic.'

Reality: JPA needs a way to set fields — either field access (no setter) or protected setters. Protected keeps callers out while letting JPA reflect. Records work with Hibernate 6+ for non-mutable value objects.

Even cleaner: separate domain model from JPA entity (Clean Architecture style) and avoid the conflict.

**When anemic is actually fine**

- DTOs: transfer data across boundaries. Pure data, no behavior. Records
- Read models / projections: built from events for queries. Pure data; query API is the behavior
- Trivial CRUD entities like Country lookup table
- Configuration / metadata objects

Smell isn't 'class without behavior' — it's 'class with behavior elsewhere that should be on it.'

**Tell-don't-ask heuristic**

Asking (anemic): caller checks getStatus, decides, calls setStatus. Rules outside the object.
Telling (rich): order.submit(); validates internally, throws if invalid. Rules live with data.

If services are full of 'if entity.getX == ... entity.setY' blocks, entity is anemic and service is doing the entity's job.

**Common mistakes**

- Calling something rich because it has methods — isShipped() that just returns status==SHIPPED is still anemic
- Using setters from anywhere — even with cancel(), leaving setStatus public lets callers bypass invariants
- Splitting one aggregate's logic across multiple objects (Order + OrderHelper + OrderValidator) — defeats encapsulation
- Persistence concerns in business methods — order.cancel() shouldn't call orderRepo.save
- Treating value objects as too small to bother — Money(amount, currency) preventing USD+EUR addition is the textbook win
- Refactoring to rich without DDD intent — just renaming doesn't fix poorly modeled aggregates

**Recommendation**

**Build rich domain models for entities and aggregates that have real business behavior — enforce invariants in constructors, use named business methods (order.cancel(), order.submit()), avoid public setters, and recompute derived state inside the entity. Use protected setters or field access for JPA when the entity is also a JPA entity, or separate domain entities from JPA entities entirely (Clean Architecture style). Anemic is fine for DTOs, read models, and trivial lookup tables — not everything needs behavior. The litmus test: 'tell, don't ask.' If your services are full of 'if entity.getX...' branches mutating the entity, your entity is anemic.**

questions.question: How do you write unit tests for a Clean Architecture application in Java?
questions.title: Unit Testing Clean Architecture in Java
questions.direct_answer: In Clean Architecture, **unit tests target each layer with the right tool:** **Entities and value objects** — plain JUnit, no framework. **Use cases (interactors)** — plain JUnit + in-memory port implementations (preferred over Mockito mocks). **Web adapters** — Spring's `@WebMvcTest` slice with mocked use cases. **Persistence adapters** — Testcontainers + real Postgres (not H2). **External adapters** — WireMock for HTTP gateways. Use `@SpringBootTest` sparingly for end-to-end smoke tests of critical flows. The result: most logic tested in milliseconds without a Spring context.

interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Using `@SpringBootTest` for everything (slow), or mocking every method on every dependency (brittle, low-signal tests).

sections.title: Why Clean Architecture Helps Testing
sections.content:
Clean Architecture's dependency rule pays the biggest dividend at test time:

- **Entities and use cases have zero framework dependencies** — they test with plain JUnit in milliseconds.
- **Adapters are the only place where infrastructure runs** — you can test them in slices without spinning up the full app.
- **Tests pyramid naturally:** thousands of fast unit tests for business logic, hundreds of slice tests for adapters, dozens of integration tests for end-to-end.

A monolithic `@SpringBootTest`-everywhere project might run 500 tests in 8 minutes. The same logic in Clean Architecture runs 5,000 tests in 90 seconds, with most failing fast and pointing exactly to the broken layer.

Layer 2 — Use Cases (Interactors)
Layer 3 — Web Adapter (`@WebMvcTest`)
Layer 4 — Persistence Adapter (Testcontainers)
Layer 5 — External Adapters (WireMock / Contract Tests)
When to Use `@SpringBootTest`
Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **`@SpringBootTest` for everything.** Pyramid inverts; CI takes 30 minutes.
- **Mocking 10 methods on 3 dependencies.** Tests break on every refactor; signal-to-noise low.
- **H2 instead of Testcontainers.** Different SQL dialect = production-only bugs.
- **Testing through controllers what the use case test should cover.** Slow, redundant, fragile.
- **No fakes for ports.** Re-mocking the same dependency in every test.
- **No tests for exception paths.** Happy-path-only tests miss the most important behavior.
- **Coverage as a goal.** 100% coverage of getters/setters tells you nothing; a high-quality test suite has lower coverage on trivia and complete coverage on logic.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Entities + use cases:** plain JUnit, in-memory ports. Microseconds per test.
- **Web adapter:** `@WebMvcTest` slice with mocked use case.
- **Persistence adapter:** Testcontainers + real DB (not H2).
- **External adapter:** WireMock + contract tests where critical.
- **`@SpringBootTest` sparingly** — only for critical end-to-end smoke tests.
- **Fakes (in-memory ports) > mocks** for use case tests — less brittle.
- **Test by layer with the right tool;** the pyramid stays right-side-up.
- **Speed matters:** fast tests run often; slow tests get skipped.

sections.content:
**Why Clean Architecture helps testing**

Dependency rule pays the biggest dividend at test time. Entities and use cases have zero framework dependencies — plain JUnit in milliseconds. Adapters are the only place where infrastructure runs — test in slices without full app.

Tests pyramid naturally: thousands of fast unit tests for business logic, hundreds of slice tests for adapters, dozens of integration tests for end-to-end.

**Layer 1 — Entities + value objects**

Plain JUnit + AssertJ. No Spring, no Mockito, no DB. Test invariants in constructors, behavior of business methods, value object equality. Microseconds per test, bulk of the suite, covers logic-dense code.

**Layer 2 — Use cases (interactors)**

Plain JUnit + in-memory implementations of ports. Why fakes over mocks: fakes behave like real adapters, work across multiple calls, tests are behavior-focused not implementation-coupled. Mocking 8 methods on 3 dependencies is brittle.

InMemoryOrderRepository, InMemoryInventoryGateway implementing the ports. PlaceOrderInteractorTest constructs them directly, calls use case, asserts side effects. No Spring, no @SpringBootTest. 100 tests in under a second.

**Layer 3 — Web adapter (@WebMvcTest)**

Spring slice loading only the web layer — controllers, exception handlers, validators. Not full app context.

Test request mapping, validation, JSON serialization, status codes, error handling. Not business logic — use case tests cover that.

@WebMvcTest(OrderController.class), @MockBean for the use case, MockMvc for the request. Fast (1-2s for slice).

**Layer 4 — Persistence adapter (Testcontainers)**

Testcontainers + real Postgres. Avoid H2 — different SQL dialect, tests pass that fail in production.

Test mapper between domain and JPA entity, repository queries, native queries, transaction behavior.

@DataJpaTest + @Testcontainers + PostgreSQLContainer. Real Postgres catches dialect issues.

**Layer 5 — External adapters**

WireMock for HTTP gateways, embedded brokers for Kafka. Stub Stripe response, verify gateway parses it. Test card-declined error path.

For critical externals, contract tests (Pact, Spring Cloud Contract) catch schema changes.

**When to use @SpringBootTest**

Sparingly — for critical end-to-end smoke tests. Goals: verify wiring works (all beans resolve, profiles load, security config OK), verify happy-path goes HTTP → use case → DB → response.

5-10 tests, not 500. Slow tests = ignored tests.

**Common mistakes**

- @SpringBootTest for everything — pyramid inverts, CI takes 30 minutes
- Mocking 10 methods on 3 dependencies — brittle, breaks on every refactor
- H2 instead of Testcontainers — production-only bugs
- Testing through controllers what use case test should cover — slow, redundant, fragile
- No fakes for ports — re-mocking same dependency every test
- No tests for exception paths — happy-path only misses important behavior
- Coverage as a goal — 100% on getters/setters tells you nothing

**Recommendation**

**Test by layer with the right tool. Plain JUnit + in-memory port implementations for entities and use cases (microseconds, the bulk of the suite). Spring slices (@WebMvcTest, @DataJpaTest with Testcontainers) for adapters. WireMock + contract tests for external dependencies. Reserve @SpringBootTest for 5-10 critical end-to-end smoke tests. Prefer fakes over mocks for use cases — less brittle, more behavior-focused. Avoid H2 in favor of Testcontainers + the real DB engine. Speed matters: a fast test suite gets run on every save; a slow one gets skipped, and the value disappears.**

questions.question: What is the difference between Clean Architecture and traditional Layered (N-tier) Architecture?
questions.title: Clean Architecture vs Layered (N-tier) Architecture
questions.direct_answer: **Layered architecture** organizes code in **horizontal stacks** (controller → service → repository → DB) where **each layer depends on the layer below**, and the **DB sits at the foundation** — the whole app is built around the database. **Clean Architecture** organizes code in **concentric circles** with the **domain at the center** and **dependencies pointing only inward** — the DB is just one of many adapters on the outside, and the domain depends on nothing. Layered is simpler and ubiquitous; Clean Architecture isolates business logic from frameworks and gives you pure-unit testability and easy adapter swaps.

interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Saying 'Clean Architecture is just layered with extra interfaces' — the dependency direction is fundamentally different.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Discuss migration paths, when to graduate, multi-input adapter benefit, and the relationship to Hexagonal/Onion.

sections.title: Two Mental Models
sections.content:
**Layered (N-tier):** stack of horizontal slices.
```
Controller → Service → Repository → Database
```
- Dependencies flow downward.
- DB sits at the base; domain depends on JPA / framework features.
- Whole app is built **around the database**.
- Most popular Spring Boot pattern.

**Clean Architecture:** concentric circles, domain-centric.
```
Frameworks (outer) → Interface Adapters → Use Cases → Entities (inner)
```
- Dependencies flow inward.
- Domain at center; framework on the outside.
- Whole app is built **around the domain**.
- DB is one of many possible adapters.

sections.title: Same Use Case in Both
What Clean Architecture Adds
sections.content:
**1. Framework independence in the core.**
- No `@Entity`, `@Transactional`, `@Service` in the domain or use cases.
- Swap Spring for Quarkus, JPA for Mongo, REST for gRPC — inner layers don't change.

**2. Pure-unit testability.**
- Test use cases with plain JUnit + in-memory port. Milliseconds.
- No `@SpringBootTest`, no Testcontainers, no H2.

**3. Multiple input adapters share business logic.**
- HTTP + Kafka consumer + scheduled job + CLI all call the same `PlaceOrderUseCase`.
- In layered, you'd often duplicate or contort the service.

**4. Explicit boundaries.**
- Ports document exactly what the core needs from infrastructure.
- Onboarding: 'these 8 ports describe everything the domain needs.'

**5. Migration safety.**
- Replacing Postgres with Mongo = replace adapter; domain logic + tests untouched.

sections.title: What Layered Keeps Cheaper
sections.content:
**1. Less code.**
- Fewer interfaces, fewer mappers, fewer packages.
- For a 5-endpoint CRUD service, half the lines.

**2. Familiarity.**
- Spring tutorials default to layered; most Java devs read it on day one.
- Lower onboarding cost in typical Spring shops.

**3. Direct framework leverage.**
- Spring Data JPA's magic methods, projections, `@EntityGraph` — right at the service layer.
- No mapping tax for simple cases.

**4. Faster prototyping.**
- POC, internal tool, MVP — layered ships in hours; Clean Architecture wants the port/adapter scaffold first.

sections.title: When to Choose Which
sections.content:
**Choose layered when:**
- CRUD-heavy with thin business logic.
- One input adapter (just HTTP).
- Small team / small service.
- Speed-of-development beats long-term flexibility.
- Team comfortable with classic Spring conventions.

**Choose Clean Architecture when:**
- Rich domain logic — a real domain model that deserves protection from framework concerns.
- Multiple input adapters share use cases (HTTP + Kafka + CRON).
- Testability without infrastructure is required (long suites that need to be fast).
- Long-lived service likely to outlive its current framework / DB choice.
- Pairing with DDD.

**Migration path layered → Clean Architecture:**
1. Extract use case interfaces from existing services.
2. Move pure domain logic into framework-free domain classes (entities, value objects).
3. Define repository ports; rename existing Spring Data interfaces to `JpaXxxRepository` and have them implement the port via a small adapter class.
4. Move mappers (DTO ↔ domain, JPA entity ↔ domain) into adapter packages.
5. Add unit tests using in-memory ports.
6. Repeat per bounded context.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Calling layered + a few interfaces 'Clean Architecture'.** The interface direction matters; it's only Clean if the *core defines the contract*.
- **Treating Clean as gospel for tiny services.** A 4-endpoint CRUD doesn't need 12 use cases and 5 ports.
- **Spring annotations leaking inward.** `@Service` on use cases or `@Entity` on domain objects defeats the point.
- **Duplicating domain entities and JPA entities just because Clean says so** — sometimes the same record works for both. Keep duplication only when domain rules / lifecycle differ.
- **Forgetting that Spring still fits.** Clean Architecture isn't anti-Spring; Spring lives in the adapter layer (controllers, repositories, configurations) and wires the core.
- **Defining a port per repository method.** Ports group cohesive behavior; don't fragment.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Layered:** dependencies flow toward DB; domain depends on framework.
- **Clean Architecture:** dependencies flow toward domain; domain depends on nothing.
- **Ports** owned by inner layers; **adapters** in outer layers implement them.
- **Clean gives you:** framework independence, pure-unit testability, easy adapter swaps, multi-input support.
- **Layered gives you:** less code, faster prototyping, familiar conventions.
- **Choose layered for CRUD;** choose Clean for rich domains, multi-adapter, or long-lived services.
- **Spring fits Clean Architecture** — it just lives in adapters, not in the core.
- **Migration is incremental** — extract use cases and ports one bounded context at a time.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
**Two mental models**

Layered: stack of horizontal slices. Controller → Service → Repository → Database. Dependencies flow downward. DB at the base. Domain depends on JPA/framework. Whole app built around the database. Most popular Spring Boot pattern.

Clean Architecture: concentric circles, domain-centric. Frameworks (outer) → Interface Adapters → Use Cases → Entities (inner). Dependencies flow inward. Domain at center, framework on outside. DB is one of many possible adapters.

**Same use case in both**

Layered: @Service with @Autowired OrderRepository (Spring Data interface). Returns OrderEntity (@Entity). Domain coupled to JPA.

Clean: PlaceOrderInteractor in inner layer, plain Java, depends on OrderRepository port. Domain Order is a record. JpaOrderRepository in adapter layer implements the port, converts between domain Order and JPA entity.

**What Clean adds**

- Framework independence: no @Entity, @Transactional in inner circles. Swap Spring → Quarkus, JPA → Mongo — inner layers don't change
- Pure-unit testability: plain JUnit + in-memory port; no @SpringBootTest, no Testcontainers. Milliseconds
- Multiple input adapters share business logic: HTTP + Kafka + CRON all call PlaceOrderUseCase
- Explicit boundaries: ports document what the core needs
- Migration safety: replace Postgres with Mongo = replace adapter; domain logic + tests untouched

**What layered keeps cheaper**

- Less code: fewer interfaces, mappers, packages. For 5-endpoint CRUD, half the lines
- Familiarity: Spring tutorials default to layered
- Direct framework leverage: Spring Data magic methods at the service
- Faster prototyping: POC ships in hours

**When to choose which**

Layered: CRUD-heavy thin business logic, one input adapter, small team/service, speed > flexibility, team comfortable with Spring conventions.

Clean: rich domain logic, multiple input adapters share use cases, testability without infrastructure required, long-lived service, pairing with DDD.

**Migration path layered → Clean**

1. Extract use case interfaces from services
2. Move pure domain logic into framework-free classes
3. Define repository ports; existing Spring Data interfaces become JpaXxxRepository, adapter implements port
4. Mappers (DTO ↔ domain, JPA entity ↔ domain) into adapter packages
5. Add unit tests with in-memory ports
6. Repeat per bounded context

**Common mistakes**

- Calling layered-with-interfaces 'Clean' — only Clean if core defines the contract
- Clean as gospel for tiny services — 4 endpoints don't need 12 use cases
- Spring annotations leaking inward — @Service on use case, @Entity on domain object
- Duplicating domain and JPA entities dogmatically — sometimes one record works for both
- Thinking Clean is anti-Spring — Spring lives in adapters and wires the core
- One port per repository method — group cohesive behavior

**Recommendation**

**Default to layered for CRUD-heavy Spring Boot services where business logic is thin, the team is small, and time-to-prototype matters. Reach for Clean Architecture (or Hexagonal — same family) when the domain is rich, multiple input adapters share use cases, fast pure-unit testing of business logic is critical, or you're pairing with DDD. The two are not enemies — Clean still uses Spring; Spring just lives in the adapters, not the core. Migrate incrementally one bounded context at a time, never as a big-bang rewrite.**

questions.question: How do you handle cross-cutting concerns like logging, security, and transactions in Clean Architecture?
questions.title: Cross-Cutting Concerns in Clean Architecture
questions.direct_answer: Cross-cutting concerns in Clean Architecture should **live at the boundary** — in the adapter layer, in `@Configuration`, or via AOP — **not inside use cases or entities**. Use **Spring AOP / interceptors** for logging, metrics, and tracing. Use **Spring Security at the web adapter** for authentication and edge authorization. Use **Spring's `@Transactional` on the use case implementation** (or wrap interactors with a transactional proxy) for atomicity. The principle: business logic stays framework-free; cross-cutting infrastructure stays in the outer rings, woven in transparently.

interviewer_intent.testing: Where cross-cutting concerns belong in a Clean Architecture project, how AOP/interceptors satisfy them without polluting the inner layers, and the pragmatic compromises (e.g., @Transactional on the interactor).
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Adding @Transactional / @PreAuthorize / Logger calls inside use cases, defeating the framework-free goal.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Discuss authorization layers (edge vs domain), distributed tracing across adapters, and the difference between policy (where) and enforcement (how) for cross-cutting concerns.

sections.title: The Principle
sections.content:
Cross-cutting concerns appear in many places in an app:
- Logging
- Metrics / monitoring
- Distributed tracing
- Authentication
- Authorization (edge + domain-level)
- Transactions
- Auditing
- Rate limiting
- Caching
- Request validation

Clean Architecture's rule: **inner layers shouldn't know about infrastructure concerns**. So:
- Don't put `Logger.info(...)` calls inside use cases.
- Don't annotate use cases with `@PreAuthorize`.
- Don't put `@Transactional` inside an entity method.

Instead, **handle cross-cutting concerns at the boundary** (controllers, adapters, configuration) or weave them in **transparently via AOP / interceptors**. The use case stays focused on business logic.

sections.title: Logging — AOP at the Boundary
Metrics and Tracing — OpenTelemetry / Micrometer
Authentication — Spring Security at the Web Adapter
Authorization — Edge vs Domain
Transactions — At the Use Case Boundary
Auditing, Caching, Validation — Same Pattern
sections.content:
**Auditing:**
- AOP aspect on use cases logs `(user, action, timestamp, result)` to an audit table.
- Or: domain emits `OrderCancelled` event; adapter consumes and writes to audit.
- Either way, use case doesn't know it's being audited.

**Caching:**
- `@Cacheable` belongs in the **adapter implementation of a query port**, not on the use case.
- The use case asks the port; the JPA-backed adapter has its own caching strategy.

**Validation (input):**
- HTTP-level validation (JSR-303 `@Valid`, `@NotBlank`) at the controller — catches malformed requests.
- Business validation (must own the order, item must be in stock) inside the entity / use case.
- Two layers, two purposes. Don't conflate.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **`@Transactional` on the controller.** Wrong layer; use case is the right boundary.
- **`@PreAuthorize` on the use case.** Couples to Spring Security; harder to test. Use it on the controller for edge auth, plain Java check inside the entity for domain auth.
- **Manually logging at every step inside the use case.** Use AOP; log at boundaries.
- **Caching results inside the use case.** Belongs in the adapter (the thing that knows how expensive the underlying call is).
- **Validating business rules in the controller** (e.g., 'is this user allowed to cancel?'). Belongs in the entity or use case; controller does input validation only.
- **AOP for everything.** Some concerns are simple enough to live as explicit calls; AOP only when the cross-cutting nature is clear.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Cross-cutting concerns belong at the boundary** — adapters, configuration, AOP — not inside use cases.
- **Logging / metrics / tracing:** AOP aspect on use cases, OpenTelemetry instrumentation in adapters.
- **Authentication:** Spring Security at the web adapter; pass plain `userId` to the use case.
- **Authorization:** edge (Spring Security on controller) for role-based; domain (explicit check inside entity / use case) for fine-grained business rules.
- **Transactions:** `@Transactional` on the use case implementation (pragmatic) or via configuration-wrapped proxy (purer).
- **Caching:** in the adapter, not in the use case.
- **Validation:** input at the controller; business rules in the entity / use case.
- **The use case stays focused on business logic;** infrastructure is woven in transparently.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
**The principle**

Cross-cutting concerns appear everywhere: logging, metrics, tracing, authentication, authorization, transactions, auditing, rate limiting, caching, validation.

Clean Architecture's rule: inner layers shouldn't know about infrastructure. Don't put Logger.info in use cases. Don't annotate use cases with @PreAuthorize. Don't put @Transactional inside entity methods.

Instead: handle at the boundary (controllers, adapters, configuration) or weave in transparently via AOP/interceptors. Use case stays focused on business logic.

**Logging — AOP at the boundary**

Don't sprinkle log.info inside business logic. AOP aspect at execution(* com.example.application.service..*.*(..)). Around advice logs USECASE_START, duration, USECASE_END, errors.

Use cases log-free, just business logic. Logging policy in one place, consistent across all use cases. Adapters have their own logging for adapter-specific concerns (HTTP, DB query timing).

Inside the domain — if logging an event is part of the business rule (audit), emit a domain event instead of calling a logger.

**Metrics and tracing — OpenTelemetry/Micrometer**

Same approach: instrument at boundary. AOP aspect for use case timer with name + status tag.

Distributed tracing: adapters create/propagate spans (HTTP middleware automatic, Kafka consumer extracts trace context from headers). OpenTelemetry auto-instrumentation handles JDBC, HTTP client. Use case is inside a span automatically; never imports OpenTelemetry.

**Authentication — Spring Security at the web adapter**

Authentication is a web-adapter concern. Spring Security validates JWT/session, builds Principal.

Controller extracts user ID from Spring Security context and passes to use case as plain string. Use case sees only customerId: String — doesn't know JWT, session, or Spring Security.

**Authorization — edge vs domain**

Two layers:

Edge/endpoint-level (web adapter): coarse role-based, 'only admins can call /admin/*'. Spring Security @PreAuthorize on controller. Stops unauthenticated/wrong-role at the door.

Domain/fine-grained (entity/use case): 'a user can cancel only their own order'. Belongs in the entity as explicit business rule. cancel(requestingUserId) checks customerId.equals(requestingUserId).

Why split: edge security is policy (can this caller hit this URL?). Domain authorization is business rule (can this user perform this action on this object?). Mixing in one annotation hides intent.

**Transactions — at the use case boundary**

User goal = business transaction. Use case is the natural boundary.

Pattern A (pragmatic, common): @Transactional on the interactor implementation. Mild Spring contamination but only one annotation, in implementation file, not port interface.

Pattern B (purer): wrap interactor with transactional proxy in @Configuration. Interactor stays Spring-free, transactional behavior added by configuration.

Pattern C (purist): UnitOfWork interface in inner layer, Spring-backed implementation in adapter. Use case explicitly uses unitOfWork.execute(() → ...). Heaviest, cleanest.

Most teams pick Pattern A. Boundary stays at the use case — that's the architectural goal.

**Auditing, caching, validation**

Auditing: AOP aspect on use cases logs (user, action, timestamp, result) to audit table. Or domain emits OrderCancelled event, adapter writes to audit.

Caching: @Cacheable in adapter implementation of a query port, not on use case. Use case asks the port; adapter has its caching strategy.

Validation: HTTP-level (JSR-303 @Valid, @NotBlank) at controller for malformed requests. Business validation (must own order, item must be in stock) inside entity/use case. Two layers, two purposes.

**Common mistakes**

- @Transactional on controller — wrong layer, use case is the right boundary
- @PreAuthorize on use case — couples to Spring Security; controller for edge, plain Java check in entity for domain auth
- Manual logging at every step in use case — use AOP, log at boundaries
- Caching inside use case — belongs in adapter
- Business rules in controller — belongs in entity/use case
- AOP for everything — some concerns are simple enough to live as explicit calls

**Recommendation**

**Keep cross-cutting concerns out of use cases and entities. Put them at the adapter boundary (Spring Security, request validation in controllers; caching, retries in repository adapters), in @Configuration (transactional proxies), or via AOP aspects (logging, metrics, tracing, auditing). For authorization, split: coarse role-based at the web adapter, fine-grained business rules inside the entity. Put @Transactional on the use case implementation (pragmatic) or wrap via configuration (purer). The principle is consistent: business logic stays framework-free; infrastructure is woven in transparently from the outer rings.**

questions.question: How does the Repository pattern work in Clean Architecture, and how is it different from Spring Data JPA?
questions.title: Repository Pattern in Clean Architecture vs Spring Data JPA
questions.direct_answer: In Clean Architecture, a **Repository is a port (interface) defined by the use case layer**, written in the **domain's vocabulary**, returning **domain objects**. The implementation lives in the **persistence adapter** — it can use Spring Data JPA, JDBC, MongoDB, or in-memory — and translates between domain entities and the underlying storage. Spring Data JPA's `JpaRepository` is **infrastructure**, not a domain repository; in Clean Architecture you wrap it inside an adapter that implements your port. This separation lets you switch persistence technologies without touching the domain.

interviewer_intent.testing: Repository as a domain abstraction (port) vs an infrastructure interface (Spring Data JPA), why the inner layer owns the contract, and the mapping between domain entities and JPA entities.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Treating Spring Data JPA's interface as the domain repository, leaking JPA into the use case layer.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Discuss aggregate-level repositories (vs CRUD per table), specification pattern, query methods on repositories vs separate query handlers (CQRS), and how to handle complex queries without leaking infrastructure.

sections.title: What a Repository Is in Clean Architecture
sections.content:
A repository in Clean Architecture (and DDD) is a **collection-like abstraction** for retrieving and persisting domain objects (typically aggregates). It exposes the operations the domain needs:
- `save(order)`
- `findById(id)`
- `findByIdempotencyKey(key)`
- `delete(order)`

It does **not** expose:
- JPA-specific things (`@Query`, criteria API, EntityGraph).
- Infrastructure details (connection pool, paging API specific to a DB).
- Generic CRUD shaped by the storage rather than the domain.

**The repository interface lives in the use case (application) layer.** The implementation lives in the persistence adapter. The domain depends on the interface, not the implementation.

sections.title: Spring Data JPA — What It Actually Is
Repository Port + Adapter — The Right Setup
Aggregate-Per-Repository, Not Table-Per-Repository
sections.content:
Spring Data tutorials suggest one repository per `@Entity`. In Clean Architecture / DDD, the repository operates on an **aggregate** — a cluster of objects treated as one consistency boundary.

**Anti-pattern:**
```java
OrderRepository, OrderItemRepository, OrderShipmentRepository, OrderPaymentRepository
```
Four repositories for one logical aggregate. Use cases need to coordinate four to save one order.

**Right shape:**
```java
OrderRepository  // saves Order with items, shipment, and payment as one unit
```

The persistence adapter maps the aggregate to multiple JPA entities behind the scenes. The use case sees one save, one transaction, one consistency boundary.

**Aggregate root:** the only entity a repository persists directly. Other objects in the aggregate are reachable through it (`order.items`, `order.shipment`).

sections.title: Complex Queries — Two Approaches
When to Use Spring Data Directly (And When Not)
sections.content:
**Use Spring Data directly (no port wrapping) when:**
- It's not a domain aggregate — a lookup table (`Country`, `Currency`).
- Read-only DTO projections for query screens (not part of the domain model).
- Internal service that doesn't aspire to Clean Architecture rigor.

**Wrap behind a port when:**
- It's a domain aggregate / entity.
- The use case layer needs to be framework-free.
- You might swap persistence technology.
- You want pure-unit tests on use cases.

Clean Architecture isn't a religious decision — it's a *cost-benefit* one. Wrapping every JPA call has a cost. Pay it for aggregates; skip it for trivial lookups.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Use case layer importing `JpaRepository`.** Defeats the purpose; JPA leaks upward.
- **Repository per JPA entity.** Should be per aggregate, often spanning multiple JPA entities.
- **Returning JPA entities from the repository port.** Then the use case is still coupled to JPA (via `OrderEntity` with lazy fields).
- **CRUD-style repository.** A `findAll()` method that returns 1M rows is irresponsible — repositories should expose use-case-driven queries, not generic CRUD.
- **Putting business logic in the repository.** Repositories persist; they don't decide. The use case calls the repository after applying business rules.
- **No mapping between domain and JPA entities.** The single-class-for-both saves a file but leaks JPA concerns into business logic.
- **Specification / Criteria API in the use case.** Use case asks the port; adapter handles the query.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Repository in Clean Architecture is a port** owned by the use case layer.
- **Spring Data `JpaRepository` is infrastructure**, not a domain repository — wrap it.
- **One repository per aggregate**, not per JPA entity.
- **Repository returns domain objects**, not JPA entities.
- **Adapter maps** domain ↔ JPA entity using a mapper.
- **Complex queries:** add finder methods sparingly, or use CQRS-style query services.
- **Don't over-apply** — trivial lookups can use Spring Data directly.
- **Repository persists; doesn't decide** — business logic in entity / use case.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
**What a repository is in Clean Architecture**

Collection-like abstraction for retrieving and persisting domain objects (typically aggregates). Exposes operations the domain needs: save(order), findById(id), findByIdempotencyKey(key), delete(order).

Does not expose: JPA-specific things (@Query, criteria API), infrastructure details (connection pool, paging APIs), generic CRUD shaped by storage rather than domain.

Repository interface lives in the use case (application) layer. Implementation lives in persistence adapter. Domain depends on interface, not implementation.

**Spring Data JPA — what it actually is**

JpaRepository<OrderEntity, String> is a Spring Data infrastructure interface. Knows about JPA, returns JPA entities, lifecycle tied to persistence context, methods like findByCustomerIdAndStatus translated into JPQL.

Great productivity tool for the persistence adapter — not the domain repository. Treating it as the domain repository leaks JPA into the use case. JPA entities with lazy proxies become domain objects; you've coupled business logic to persistence framework.

In Clean Architecture, JpaRepository is hidden behind the adapter — useful tool to implement the port, never the port itself.

**Repository port + adapter — the right setup**

Application layer: OrderRepository interface with save, findById, findByIdempotencyKey, findActiveByCustomerId. Returns domain Order.

Adapter layer: OrderJpaEntity (@Entity, @Table, @OneToMany on items). OrderSpringRepo extends JpaRepository<OrderJpaEntity, String> with JPA-specific finders. JpaOrderRepository implements OrderRepository, uses OrderSpringRepo + OrderMapper to convert.

Use cases depend on OrderRepository. JPA invisible above the adapter.

**Aggregate-per-repository, not table-per-repository**

Spring Data tutorials suggest one repository per @Entity. In Clean Architecture/DDD, repository operates on an aggregate — cluster of objects treated as one consistency boundary.

Anti-pattern: OrderRepository + OrderItemRepository + OrderShipmentRepository + OrderPaymentRepository. Four for one logical aggregate.

Right: just OrderRepository, saves Order with items, shipment, payment as one unit. Persistence adapter maps to multiple JPA entities behind the scenes.

Aggregate root: only entity a repository persists directly. Other objects reachable through it (order.items, order.shipment).

**Complex queries — two approaches**

Approach 1: add finder methods to the repository. findActiveByCustomerId, findOverdueByDueDate. Fine for a handful, doesn't scale to dozens of report-style queries.

Approach 2: CQRS-style separate query interfaces. OrderQueryService.findSummary(orderId), search(criteria, page), monthlyStats(month). Returns DTOs, not domain objects. Implementation can use SQL views, projections, separate read model. Keeps write-side OrderRepository focused on the aggregate's lifecycle.

For read-heavy systems with complex query needs, separating commands from queries (CQRS lite) is the practical choice. Don't try to express every query as a domain repository method.

**When to use Spring Data directly**

Directly when: not a domain aggregate (Country, Currency lookup table), read-only DTO projections for query screens, internal service that doesn't aspire to Clean Architecture rigor.

Wrap behind a port when: domain aggregate/entity, use case layer needs to be framework-free, might swap persistence technology, pure-unit tests on use cases.

Clean Architecture isn't religious — it's cost-benefit. Wrapping every JPA call has a cost. Pay it for aggregates; skip it for trivial lookups.

**Common mistakes**

- Use case importing JpaRepository — JPA leaks upward
- Repository per JPA entity — should be per aggregate
- Returning JPA entities from repository port — use case still coupled
- CRUD-style repository with findAll returning 1M rows
- Business logic in repository — repositories persist, don't decide
- No mapping between domain and JPA entities — leaks JPA concerns
- Specification/Criteria API in use case — adapter handles the query

**Recommendation**

**Define repositories as ports owned by the use case layer, written in domain vocabulary, returning domain objects. Implement them in the persistence adapter using Spring Data JPA as the underlying tool — wrap, don't expose. One repository per aggregate (not per table). For complex query needs, add CQRS-style query services that return DTOs and can hit projections or SQL views directly. Don't over-apply: trivial lookup tables can use Spring Data directly without a port. The discipline pays off for aggregates with real business behavior; for read-only DTOs, the wrapping is overhead.**

questions.title: When NOT to Use Clean Architecture
questions.direct_answer: Skip Clean Architecture when its costs outweigh its benefits: **simple CRUD apps**, **short-lived services or POCs**, **tiny teams** where coordination cost is zero, **services with one input adapter and a stable framework choice**, and **infrastructure-heavy services** where business logic is thin (ETL pipelines, log processors). Clean Architecture's value — framework independence, pure-unit testability, multi-adapter reuse — only pays back when those things matter. Forcing it on simple apps creates ceremony, mappers, and packages that slow delivery without providing benefit.
