sections.title: What Clean Architecture Costs You
sections.content:
Clean Architecture isn't free. Real costs:

- **More files per feature.** A simple CRUD endpoint might need: controller, request DTO, response DTO, use case interface, command DTO, response DTO (use case shape), interactor implementation, repository port, JPA entity, JPA Spring repo, mapper, adapter implementation. Twelve files where layered would have three.
- **Mapping tax.** Domain entity ↔ JPA entity ↔ DTO conversions add code, tests, and the chance of mapping bugs.
- **Onboarding time.** New devs accustomed to Spring tutorials need to learn the ports/adapters mental model.
- **Slower prototyping.** Adding a new field touches more files.
- **Configuration overhead.** `@Configuration` beans wiring ports to implementations; ArchUnit rules to enforce boundaries.

These costs pay back when the architecture's benefits matter. When they don't, you've added overhead with no return.

sections.title: Signal 1 — Simple CRUD with Thin Business Logic
sections.content:
If your service is mostly:
- HTTP → validate → persist → respond.
- Or: HTTP → read → transform to DTO → respond.

...then Clean Architecture's investment in protecting the domain doesn't pay off because **there's no domain to protect**. The 'business logic' is field validation and SQL.

**Examples:**
- Admin dashboard backend.
- Lookup / reference data service.
- Simple internal tools.
- A microservice that just exposes an existing DB table over REST.

**Better choice:** layered Spring Boot. `@RestController` → `@Service` → `JpaRepository`. Three files per feature. Ship in days.

sections.title: Signal 2 — Short-Lived Service / POC / Demo
sections.content:
If the service will live weeks (POC, hackathon, internal experiment, throwaway integration), the long-term benefits of Clean Architecture (swap framework, swap DB, evolve over years) never materialize.

**Cost-benefit:** Clean Architecture pays back over **months to years**. POCs don't have months.

**Better choice:** the simplest layered structure that ships. Clean code, but not Clean Architecture.

**Caveat:** sometimes a 'POC' becomes production. If the team has a habit of POCs surviving, plan to refactor early or just start with a modest layered structure that's refactor-friendly.

sections.title: Signal 3 — One Input Adapter, Stable Framework Choice
sections.content:
Clean Architecture shines when:
- Multiple input adapters (HTTP + Kafka + CRON) share use cases.
- Likely to swap framework or DB someday.

If your service has:
- One input adapter (just HTTP).
- A framework choice that won't change in the foreseeable future (committed to Spring Boot for the company's lifetime).
- A DB choice that's locked in.

...then framework independence isn't valuable to you. The mapping tax exists with no payoff.

**Better choice:** layered. If the day comes that you need a Kafka adapter, you can extract use cases then — the refactor is straightforward.

sections.title: Signal 4 — Tiny Team / Low Coordination Cost
sections.content:
Clean Architecture's explicit boundaries help **multiple teams or developers** coordinate — 'these are the use cases the application offers; that's the contract.'

For a 1-2 person team where everyone knows everything, that explicit-contract benefit is small. The same person reads and writes both layers.

**Better choice:** layered. Conventions and good packaging are enough.

**Caveat:** if the team grows, the lack of architectural discipline becomes painful. Watch for the inflection point (4-6 devs) and consider a refactor.

sections.title: Signal 5 — Infrastructure-Heavy Services
sections.content:
Some services are mostly **infrastructure orchestration** with very thin business logic:
- ETL pipelines.
- Log aggregators.
- Metric exporters.
- File transformers.
- API proxies.

The domain is essentially 'move data from A to B with these rules.' A use case layer adds ceremony without abstraction value — the 'business logic' is the infrastructure.

**Better choice:** straightforward processing pipeline. Functions over classes. Maybe a clean module structure but no use cases / ports / aggregates.

sections.title: When to Reconsider — The Inflection Points
sections.content:
Watch for signals that the layered approach is straining:

- **Service classes growing past ~500 lines** — logic is scattered.
- **Same business rule duplicated** in two services.
- **Need to add a Kafka consumer** that should reuse HTTP service logic.
- **Hard to write fast unit tests** because everything needs Spring context.
- **Schema changes ripple** through controllers and DTOs.
- **Onboarding new devs gets harder** — no clear contract for what each service does.

When you see 2-3 of these, refactor incrementally to Clean Architecture (or Hexagonal). Pull use cases out of services; introduce ports for repositories. Don't big-bang.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Going Clean for everything because the team likes it.** Cost-benefit varies by service.
- **Half-applied Clean Architecture.** Use cases exist but call repositories that return JPA entities; you have ceremony without isolation. Worst of both worlds.
- **Refusing Clean Architecture even when symptoms scream for it.** A 5,000-line service class isn't a sign you should keep going.
- **Thinking 'Clean = ports/adapters/use cases'.** Sometimes 'clean code' (good packaging, separation of concerns) without the formal Clean Architecture pattern is what you really need.
- **Treating Spring as 'unclean' and trying to remove it.** Spring fits Clean Architecture; it just lives in the adapters.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Skip Clean Architecture for:** simple CRUD, short-lived services, single-adapter stable services, tiny teams, infrastructure-heavy services with thin business logic.
- **Real costs:** more files, mapping tax, onboarding, slower prototyping.
- **Apply Clean Architecture for:** rich domains, multi-adapter systems, long-lived services, large teams, framework portability needs.
- **Watch inflection points:** large service classes, duplicated rules, new adapter needs, slow tests — refactor incrementally.
- **Avoid half-applied Clean** — worst of both worlds.
- **Architecture is cost-benefit, not religion.**
